thebossmd Non-Clinical Careers , Professional Position , TheBossMD Interviews Dr. John Jurica
Welcome to episode 2 of TheBossMD Interviews! In this series, I bring you quality interviews with high impact people that can help you manage your position . Today’s interview is with Dr. John Jurica from The Vital Physician Executive . Dr. Jurica tells us about his experience pursuing non-clinical careers in his own life and how he has started a website to help other physicians take that same journey. This should be a great resource for anyone that has wondered how your skills as a physician might be used outside clinical medicine and the steps you should consider if you want to pursue that career path. Even better, read all the way to the end for a chance to win a free gift ! Please welcome Dr. Jurica! Tell us about your professional background. I graduated from the University of Illinois College of Medicine, and then completed a Family Medicine Residency affiliated with the U. of I. While practicing full-time a few years later, I obtained a Master’s Degree in Public Health from the Medical College of Wisconsin. In 2012, I became a Certified Physician Executive (CPE) through the Certifying Commission in Medical Management. I practiced family medicine for several years in a three-man group. I also worked at various times as part-time medical director for a family planning clinic, an occupational medicine medical director, and physician advisor for utilization review. I phased out of those part-time jobs, and took a position as Vice President for Medical Affairs at a hospital outside of Chicago, Illinois. I later became Chief Medical Officer and completely withdrew from clinical practice for a few years. In 2014, I left my CMO position to invest in an urgent care start-up and became medical director, where I continue to practice and supervise clinical activities of the clinic. I now devote half my work hours to the urgent care center, and the other half to producing my blog and podcast.
[TheBossMD: I’d say you are fairly experienced in the physician side gig world!] Why did you start The Vital Physician Executive? Primarily, I wanted to help motivate and support physicians seeking leadership positions. I’m a firm believer that we need more physician leaders, especially in the hospital setting. As CMO, I was part of a very aggressive, successful executive team. We were running a regional stand-alone hospital that was consistently profitable, while most of the hospitals in Illinois were losing money or barely breaking even. We had achieved (Truven) Top 100 Hospital status for several years, and multiple five-star ratings from HealthGrades. So, I knew that our approaches worked. And I wanted to share what I learned with aspiring physician executives. I liked to write, and I wanted to improve my writing, so a blog seemed to be a good way to do that. I chose the title because it reflected both the vitality needed to be a physician executive, and the fact that a good CMO is vital to a well-functioning hospital or health system. What resources do you have for physicians on your site and what value can you provide for them? The blog has over a hundred articles, most of which address topics of interest to hospital leaders. It also hosts my podcast show notes. I’ve completed 55 podcast episodes so far, the majority of which are interviews with physicians doing non-clinical work, including physician coaches. Many of the episodes serve as how-to guides, walking the listener through the process of pivoting into the featured career. Many of the posts also include transcripts that listeners can download and read at their leisure. I also offer a free guide to three nonclinical careers for those that sign up for my newsletter ( sign up here ) . The blog’s newsletters provide additional resources for my subscribers. I’ll often post links to articles or job openings in the newsletter. And, my weekly Saturday edition chronicles my efforts to create an online business. Recent issues share what I’ve learned blogging, podcasting and creating my first mentoring program.
[TheBossMD: Great value here for anyone curious about starting a website. Looking at some of the larger players in the physician website space can be intimidating and hides the extensive journey that it takes to reach that kind of status. Follow along with Dr. Jurica’s newsletter to see how the journey really looks!] Ready To Exit His Current Career Why do you think there is growing interest in non-clinical physician careers? The biggest reason is that many physicians are suffering from burnout, caused by the commoditization of medical care, loss of autonomy, excessive work hours, and our own perfectionism and deeply held sense of responsibility. There’s also the disillusionment that comes from choosing a career while we’re still adolescents and young adults, only to wake up 11 to 15 years later to find out that medicine is not what we thought it would be. There are also some very positive reasons. Many of us find that we love helping people, and that there are opportunities to do that on a much grander scale. That leads us to become health system leaders, biotechnology entrepreneurs, medical business consultants and authors or speakers. The interest in non-clinical careers has also paralleled the recognition that work-life balance is critical to maintaining physical and mental health.
[TheBossMD: I like this answer. Non-clinical careers can be an answer to burnout, but they are not reserved for those that just “want out of medicine.” Non-clinical careers often lead to opportunities to affect patient care on a much broader scale.] Do you think business degrees are necessary for physician executives? What kind of commitment does this involve? I believe seeking a business degree is generally a worthwhile commitment, but it is time-consuming and costly. And there are many capable physician executives who do not have a business degree. Luckily, physicians are very effective life-long learners. We know how to rapidly absorb information, and how to effectively use mentors. When I decided to pursue my MPH, I was already reading 5 to 10 clinical journals each week, so I devoted that time and energy to my new coursework. I believe that the CPE can substitute for the MBA, for those physicians who want to take a more flexible approach to learning. In that process, you go at your own pace, participating in business and management courses through the AAPL ( American Association for Physician Leadership? . Once you’ve completed all of the necessary courses, you complete the final “capstone” and obtain the CPE. I’ve seen the CPE mentioned in job descriptions, just as the MBA or other business degrees are. Neither is usually required. But it does help to have one, or both, if you’re applying for a competitive position. Employers generally focus first on management experience, and then on a business degree as a differentiator. An MBA or MMM (Master’s in Medical Management) will usually take 18 to 24 months to complete, and cost between $30,000 and $80,000. You can cut the costs by going to a local public university. But such a program will likely not be an executive MBA designed for physicians. There is at least one program that you can complete in one year. It’s the University of Tennessee’s Haslam School of Business Physician Executive MBA . It requires about 20 hours of study per week, though, so it can be quite intense. In order to save time and money, it’s also possible to get credit for courses from the AAPL to apply to certain affiliated MBA and MMM programs. Your readers would need to contact the AAPL directly to learn more about that.
[TheBossMD: I must admit my skepticism to some degree regarding those that say an MBA is essential for a physician wanting to pursue management opportunities. Dr. Jurica’s advice is accurate. The programs he lists are some of the well known ones, but I have seen plenty of successful physician executives without additional degrees.] What is the most interesting non-clinical physician career you have seen? As a class, I think physician entrepreneurs are very interesting. Sylvia Romm, a pediatric hospitalist, started her own part-time telehealth company. She grew that, then sold it to a large national IT company, and became one of its senior executives. You can listen to my podcast episode featuring Dr. Romm here . Needs Some Good Advice What advice would you give a physician who wants to explore non-clinical opportunities but doesn’t know where to start? Taking those first few steps can be the most daunting. Here’s my advice. You might start by assessing your personality and your readiness to begin a career pivot. Short of a formal Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory (MMPI) or Myers Brigg Type Inventory, you can access the free 16Personalities online self-assessment and the Pivotability Index on Jenny Blake’s website to help assess your readiness for career change. Next, my recommendation is to approach it like any new interest. “Devour” as much free advice and information as you can. Then move on to paid help if the free stuff doesn’t meet your needs. There are several free blogs devoted to career change. Look for Zebras is a great place to start. An article on that site links to descriptions of 19 nonclinical careers that can help physicians understand the breadth of possible nonclinical careers available. Another site that lists possible career choices is Nonclinical Doctors by Heidi Moawad, MD. She provides specific descriptions of various careers with success stories for some of them. There are also several Facebook and LinkedIn groups devoted to nonclinical careers. I am one of the administrators for the Physician Nonclinical Career Hunters Facebook Group founded by Dr. Laura McKain a few years ago. Members share information and provide resources and advice to one another. It now has over 10,000 physician members. Sometimes, however, it’s necessary to invest a little money in exchange for accelerating your career pursuits.
